Learning Objectives
Determine the importance of weight-bearing radiographs and the implications relative to
common sports injuries.
Assess standard foot/ankle radiographs and interpret common pathologies.
Compile specialized foot/ankle radiographs and demonstrate the manner in which to best use
these views.
Compare indications for foot/ankle advanced imaging studies (CT/MRI) and determine the
manner in which these modalities contribute to identifying and managing specific injuries.

Imaging of the lower extremity provides critical information in the care of athletes with knee,
ankle, and foot problems.
Plain radiographs, specialized radiographs, and advanced imaging studies (CT/MRI) have a role
complementing the patient history and physical evaluation.
Stress and weight-bearing radiographs can increase the diagnostic accuracy of imaging of the
lower extremity.

Overview
Imaging of the lower extremity provides critical information, aiding in the care of athletes
with knee, ankle, and foot problems. Although the knee is not covered in this lesson, the
joints above and below the area of clinical concern are important to examine, and this
relationship should be considered with regard to imaging the lower extremity. From
fractures and stress reactions to ligament and syndesmotic injuries, plain radiographs,
specialized radiographs, and advanced imaging studies (CT/MRI) complement the patient
history and physical examination to guide care for common and uncommon injuries.
Because of complex anatomic relationships in the foot and ankle, stress views and
weight-bearing radiographs, in addition to standard radiographs, provide additional
valuable information to clinicians. Numerous studies have demonstrated improved
diagnostic accuracy of weight-bearing radiographs in the lower extremity and changes in
radiographic parameters with weight-bearing.1-3 Finally, if weight-bearing radiographs of
the foot and ankle reveal substantial deformity, standing hip-knee-ankle radiographs
may be obtained to better characterize overall limb alignment and deformity (Figure 1).

Standard Ankle Radiographs
Standard radiographs of the ankle include AP, lateral, and mortise views.
Weight-bearing radiographs are essential, if possible, for identifying and assessing bony
alignment of the foot and ankle.


Standard Ankle Radiographs
Standard radiographs of the ankle include AP, lateral, and mortise views. Weight-bearing
radiographs are essential, if possible, for identifying and assessing bony alignment of the
foot and ankle. For example, in patients with recurrent lateral ankle instability, failure to
identify and manage cavovarus deformity may predispose patients to recurrent
instability and, ultimately, failed ligament reconstruction procedures.
The first step in interpreting standard three-view ankle radiographs is assessing the
quality of the radiograph. A standard AP ankle radiograph is obtained with the foot
parallel to the x-ray beam. In this view, the fibula shoulder is slightly superimposed over
the tibia with visible joint space of the superior talar dome and the malleoli on profile. An
ankle mortise view is obtained with the ankle internally rotated 12° to 17°, such that the
fifth metatarsal is in line with the axis of the calcaneus.4 The ankle mortise and the
medial, superior, and lateral talar joint space should be visualized clearly and
symmetrically. A lateral ankle view should clearly demonstrate the tibiotalar joint space
with symmetric overlap of the medial and lateral talar domes. On this view, the distal
fibula should superimpose the posterior tibia; however, the degree of overlap may be
variable based on patient syndesmotic anatomy.5
In interpreting standard ankle radiographs, orthopaedic surgeons should realize that an
abundance of information can be gleaned from each view. In a recent literature review
on various radiographic measures about the foot and ankle, Lamm et al6 described no
fewer than 35 different measurement criteria. Memorization of all 35 angle
measurement ranges is impractical; however, the specific radiographic evaluation should
be based on the suspected injury and physical examination findings. Surgeons should be
cognizant of general gross alignment and parameters for common pathologies. Below is
a review of commonly used radiographic measurements and signs for interpretation of
ankle radiographs:
Tibia-Fibula Clear Space

Measured 1 cm proximal to the tibial plafond, this clear space should be less than 6 mm on AP
and mortise views. A space greater than 6 mm is indicative of a syndesmotic injury.
Pneumaticos et al4 demonstrated that this parameter was the least subjective to slight
variation in patient positioning (Figure 2).
Figure 2 AP (A) and mortise (B) ankle radiographs demonstrate tibia-fibula clear space between
the yellow lines. (Courtesy of Brian C. Lau, MD, Durham, NC.)
Tibia-Fibula Overlap
Overlap of the tibia and fibula on an AP ankle view should be more than 6 mm. Overlap on a
mortise view should be more than 1 mm.7
Overlap less than these values is suggestive of syndesmotic injury (Figure 3).

5/30

Figure 3 AP (A) and mortise (B) ankle radiographs demonstrate tibia-fibula overlap between the
yellow lines. (Courtesy of Brian C. Lau, MD, Durham, NC.)
Medial Clear Space
The medial clear space, measured between the medial border of the talus and the most lateral
edge of the medial malleolus on a mortise view, should be less than 4 mm.7
Medial clear space greater than 4 mm is indicative of a deltoid ligament injury (Figure 4;
Resource 1).
SEND FEEDBACK

6/30

Figure 4 Mortise ankle radiograph demonstrates medial clear space between the yellow lines.
(Courtesy of Brian C. Lau, Durham, MD, NC.)
Dime Sign
The dime sign is visualized on a mortise view. It is an unbroken circle connecting the distal tip
of the fibula to the lateral process of the talus.8
A broken circle, or positive dime sign, is suggestive of fibular shortening (Figure 5).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:26 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Lower Extremity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001184
7/30

Figure 5 Mortise ankle radiograph demonstrates a circumferential line connecting the distal
fibula to the lateral process of the talus. (Courtesy of Brian C. Lau, MD, Durham, NC.)
Shenton Line
The Shenton line of the ankle is a continuous arc spanning from the tibial plafond laterally to
the Wagstaffe tubercle and distal along the lateral malleolus.8
Disruption of this line is suggestive of fibular shortening (Figure 6).

Figure 6 Mortise ankle radiograph demonstrates the Shenton line. (Courtesy of Brian C. Lau, MD,
Durham, NC.)
Cam Impingement
Cam impingement of the ankle is an anatomic abnormality characterized by a non-spherical
talar dome.9
The non-spherical shape results in pathologic contact between the anteromedial talus and the
anterior tibial plafond, abnormal loading of the talar dome cartilage, and eventual progression
of anteromedial talar osteophytes (Figures 3 and 7).

(Courtesy of Annunziato Amendola, MD, Durham, NC.)

Cam Impingement
Lastly, orthopaedic surgeons should be aware of the Ottawa rules but consider
themselves above the law with respect to these rules. The Ottawa rules, originally
described in 1996, were meant to guide primary care and emergency room physicians
on the timing for obtaining radiographs. The three criteria for obtaining ankle
radiographs are posteromedial malleolus tenderness, posterolateral malleolus
tenderness, or inability to bear weight.10 Although these rules are general guidelines for
minimizing the cost and radiation exposure associated with unnecessary radiographs in
urgent care and the emergency room, radiographs remain a pillar in the assessment of
sports-related ankle injuries.
Ancillary Ankle Radiographs
Ancillary radiographs of the ankle include gravity stress, external rotation stress, oblique
anteromedial impingement, hindfoot alignment, and Broden views.


Ancillary Ankle Radiographs
The standard three-view series is essential for the evaluation and diagnosis of sports
injuries to the ankle. Based on patient history and physical examination findings, unique
radiographs of the ankle may aid in making a diagnosis or further delineating ankle
alignment. Below are commonly performed supplemental views orthopaedic surgeons
should be aware of:
Gravity Stress
Gravity stress views of the ankle are obtained with the patient in the lateral decubitus position
with the injured ankle nearest the floor. The patient’s injured leg must extend beyond the
examination table to allow gravity to pull the distal fibula and talus away from the tibia.7
Asymmetry, or increased medial clear space widening beyond 5 mm, is indicative of a deltoid
injury (Figure 8).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:26 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Lower Extremity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001184
11/30

Figure 8 A, Mortise non-stress radiograph of an ankle demonstrates a symmetric tibiotalar joint.
B, Gravity stress radiograph of the same ankle demonstrates increased medial clear space
widening. (Courtesy of Brian C. Lau, MD, Durham, NC.)
External Rotation Stress
Similar to gravity stress, direct external rotation stress radiographs can be obtained by having
the examiner manually externally rotate the foot while supporting the leg.7
Increased medial clear space widening beyond 5 mm is indicative of deltoid ligament injury.
Oblique Anteromedial Impingement
This oblique view, as the name suggests, is useful for detecting anteromedial impinging
osteophytes of the talus.11
This radiograph is obtained with the x-ray beam tilted 45° craniocaudally from the standard
lateral position with the foot externally rotated 30°.
With CT-confirmed impingement, standard radiographs only detect 40% of anteromedial
osteophytes, whereas this oblique view can detect 85% of osteophytes (Resource 2).

Hindfoot Alignment View
The hindfoot alignment view is obtained from posterior to anterior with the patient standing
and the x-ray beam tilted 20° caudally.6
This view captures standing alignment from the most distal aspect of the calcaneus to the axis
of the tibia. This view allows for quantification of hindfoot alignment (Figure 9).

Broden View
The Broden view is obtained with the patient’s leg in 45° of internal rotation and the x-ray
beam tilted cephalad between 10° and 40°. This view provides clear visualization of the
posterior facet of the subtalar joint.12
Because of variations in anatomy, cephalic tilt ranges from 10° to 40°, thereby requiring
multiple attempts to zero in on the narrow corridor of the posterior facet of the subtalar joint.
This view may be helpful for diagnosing talocalcaneal coalition and subtalar arthritis and
reduction of calcaneal fractures (Figure 10).
Figure 10 Intraoperative Broden view fluoroscopic image of an ankle shows the posterior facet of

the calcaneus (yellow line). (Courtesy of Brian C. Lau, MD, Durham, NC.)
CT of the Ankle
CT of the ankle may be useful for characterizing fracture patterns, syndesmotic reduction, and
tarsal coalition.

CT of the Ankle
CT of the ankle is immensely useful for characterizing bony pathology of the ankle,
namely fractures and tumors; however, its usefulness for evaluation of cartilage,
ligamentous, and tendinous structures is somewhat limited. Regardless, CT is helpful in
patients with specific conditions.
Tarsal coalition is the pathologic process by which two joints of the foot are abnormally
joined by an osseous or fibrous bridge. The resultant pathologic union may hinder
hindfoot motion at the subtalar joint and place excess stress on the lateral ligamentous
complex of the ankle. In a review of 223 ankle sprains in athletes, Snyder et al13 found
evidence of tarsal coalition in 65%. The most common site of coalition was
calcaneonavicular. Nine percent of these coalitions were complete bony unions, whereas
the remaining were partial or fibrous/cartilaginous.
The anatomic relationship of the syndesmosis is highly variable.14 In a prospective CT
study, Liu et al15 described three general patterns or shapes of the distal tibia-fibula joint
and incisura. They summarized these into a classic C shape, an I shape, and inverted L
shape. The authors found the I shape to be associated with the highest risks of future
ankle sprains. The importance of anatomic syndesmotic reduction has gained increasing
recognition; however, the best methods of assessing syndesmotic reduction on plain
radiographs remain contested.16 In a review of 25 ankle fractures with syndesmosis
injuries managed surgically via screw fixation, radiographs failed to detect 9 of the 13
(69%) malreduced syndesmotic joints later detected via CT.17 Therefore, cross-sectional
imaging remains the preferred imaging modality for assessing syndesmotic reduction.
However, use of CT in assessing syndesmotic reduction is not always practical in all

9/3/26, 4:26 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Lower Extremity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001184
16/30

patients. A surgeon may consider CT for the postoperative assessment of syndesmotic
reduction if malreduction is suspected (patients in whom the syndesmosis has been
malreduced may warrant a return to the operating room) or for the intraoperative use of
O-arm or three-dimensional C-arm. With intraoperative CT, successful syndesmotic
reduction can be confirmed but may result in increased radiation exposure and surgical
time and elicits the question, “how many times do you assess reduction after the first CT
scan?” Therefore, the authors of this lesson recommend standard intraoperative
fluoroscopy for assessment of syndesmotic reduction and reserve CT only for patients in
whom malreduction is suspected.
Lastly, weight-bearing CT has emerged as a useful new technique to better
characterizing hindfoot alignment. In a review of weight-bearing CT scans, Conti and
Ellis18 describe the various uses for understanding bony alignment, cavovarus, hallux
valgus, and ankle fracture (Resource 3). The relationship between increased hindfoot
varus and recurrent lateral ankle instability is established but has yet to be fully
quantified. As hindfoot angular parameters continue to be measured in relation to
lateral ankle instability, weight-bearing CT scans may become a useful adjunct in surgical
planning.
MRI of the Ankle
MRI of the ankle is useful for identifying intra-articular pathology, such as chondral injury for
preoperative planning and for assessing the integrity of supporting ligaments and traversing
tendons about the ankle.

MRI of the Ankle
Patient history, physical examination, and radiographs are the mainstay of diagnosis of
ligamentous injury to the foot and ankle. Intra-articular pathology often is suspected
based on patient history and physical examination; however, MRI remains essential for
confirmation of diagnosis and quantification of chondral pathology and often is useful
for preoperative planning.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:26 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Lower Extremity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001184
17/30

Standard MRI protocols include axial, coronal, and sagittal 3-mm cuts. T1- and T2-
weighted (fluid-sensitive) images typically are obtained in all three planes. Often, specific
sequences will be added or windows will be expanded by the radiologist planning the
MRI protocol, highlighting the importance of including details such as pathology
suspected in ordering MRI. For example, an ankle MRI protocol for a calcaneal stress
fracture may include thinner slices on T1-weighted images, whereas an MRI protocol for
Achilles tendon rupture may expand the field of view to include the myotendinous
junction.
Detailing the location of each anatomical structure around the ankle joint is beyond the
scope of this lesson; however, each surgeon should develop a reproducible search
pattern to minimize missed pathology. Search patterns generally fall into one of two
categories: identifying an anatomic structure one at a time on each sequence or
identifying all anatomic structures on a given sequence then repeating on each
sequence.
In general, ligaments and tendons about the ankle are best visualized on T1-weighted
images and can be identified as thick, low-intensity bands if healthy. MRI of the ankle is
particularly useful for identifying osteochondral defects of the talus and aiding in
preoperative planning. Identification and quantification of chondral defects of the talus
typically are best visualized on T2-weighted images. In patients in whom an intact
osteochondral fragment is present, prompt identification and thoughtful planning to
approach may result in successful reduction and fixation (Figure 4). In patients in whom
no meaningful reduction can be achieved, then additional cartilage procedures, such as
microfracture, osteochondral allografting, autografting, and autologous chondrocyte
implantation, also may be considered (Figure 11).

Figure 11 Sagittal T2-weighted MRI of an ankle shows an osteochondral defect of the
talar dome with increased surrounding signal representing bone edema. (Courtesy of
Annunziato Amendola, MD, Durham, NC.)
Standard Foot Radiographs
Standard foot radiographs include AP, lateral, and oblique views.
Weight-bearing radiographs are especially important in the foot with regard to midfoot
trauma, including Lisfranc injuries.

Standard Foot Radiographs
Standard radiographs of the foot include AP, lateral, and oblique views. Weight-bearing
radiographs are equally important with regard to the foot, if possible, for assessing bony
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:26 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Lower Extremity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001184
19/30

alignment and functional measurements and dynamic or subtle instability. Most
commonly, this subtle instability is observed in patients with a Lisfranc injury to the
midfoot.
The first step in interpreting standard radiographs of the foot is evaluating the quality of
the radiograph. A standard AP foot radiograph is obtained with the x-ray beam aimed
toward the dorsum of the foot (angled 10° to 15° toward the heel). A standard lateral
foot radiograph is obtained with the x-ray beam aimed at the lateral aspect of the foot. A
30° oblique foot radiograph provides an intermediate view between AP and lateral views,
which is particularly helpful given the complex bony anatomy of the midfoot.5 Examples
of each of these standard foot radiographs are shown in Figures 5 and 12.
Close scrutiny of all three of radiographic views is critically important, especially in
patients with trauma, given the complex bony anatomy and articulations of the foot.
Surgeons should be familiar with overall alignment and parameters for common
pathologies.
Figure 12 AP (A), 30° oblique (B), and lateral (C) weight-bearing foot radiographs
demonstrate standard foot radiographs. (Courtesy of Brian C. Lau, MD, Durham, NC.)
Fifth Metatarsal Base Fractures

Fifth metatarsal base fractures are common sports injuries visualized on plain radiographs.
Zone I: fractures proximal to the articulation between the fourth and fifth metatarsals
Zone II: fractures located in the area of the bone involving the articulation between the
fourth and fifth metatarsals; fractures in this zone are at increased risk for nonunion (Figure
13).
Zone III: fractures distal to the articulation between the fourth and fifth metatarsals;
fractures in this zone may occur secondary to repetitive stress and also are at increased risk
for nonunion.
Figure 13 Oblique foot radiograph demonstrates a zone II fracture of the base of fifth metatarsal.
(Courtesy of Annunziato Amendola, MD, Durham, NC.) 

Fifth Metatarsal Base Fractures
For sports-related injuries, plain radiographs are most helpful with regard to fifth
metatarsal base fractures, commonly referred to as Jones fractures19 (Resource 4).
These fractures can be visualized, in part, on all three standard radiographic views of the
foot. Modern understanding of fifth metatarsal base fractures describes three zones of
fractures, with different implications for management and healing20:

Lisfranc Injuries
Standard radiographs must be scrutinized for midfoot (tarsometatarsal joint) trauma,
including Lisfranc injuries.
Weight-bearing radiographs and stress views may be useful to detect subtle instability.
With regard to the midfoot, the following radiographic relationships are normal and any
disruption of these relationships may be indicative of injury or instability (Figures 5 and 7)21:
AP view
The medial aspect of the second metatarsal base should be in line with the medial aspect
of the middle cuneiform.
Lateral view
The first and second tarsometatarsal joints should be concentrically reduced.
Oblique view
The medial aspect of the base of the fourth metatarsal should be in line with the medial
aspect of the cuboid.
The medial column line should be intact (a line drawn from the navicular to the medial
cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal; Figure 14).
The fleck sign is representative of a Lisfranc injury with an avulsion fracture of the Lisfranc
ligament originating on the medial cuneiform and inserting on the second metatarsal base.
Figure 14 AP (A), 30° oblique (B), and lateral (C) weight-bearing foot radiographs demonstrate

important radiographic relationships. (Courtesy of Annunziato Amendola, MD, Durham, NC.)
Weight-bearing AP view
A single weight-bearing AP view of both feet (and equal weight bearing through both feet)
obtained on the same cassette may aid in the identification of subtle Lisfranc injury.22
(Figure 15).
Figure 15 AP weight-bearing radiograph of bilateral feet on a single cassette demonstrate
widening between the base of the second metatarsal and the medial cuneiform in the left foot
compared with the normal right foot. This difference is suggestive of a subtle, purely ligamentous
Lisfranc injury. (Courtesy of Annunziato Amendola, MD, Durham, NC.)

Stress views
If weight-bearing views do not demonstrate instability but instability is suspected, then stress
views should be performed.
Manual stress radiographs revealed greater displacement than weight-bearing radiographs
for Lisfranc instability in a cadaver model.23
To perform stress views, with appropriate anesthesia or analgesia, the examiner will stabilize
the medial cuneiform and cuboid and subsequently apply forefoot abduction/abduction
forces and dorsiflexion forces.24
MRI of the foot
Also can be used to predict instability to the Lisfranc ligament/joint complex.
MRI demonstrating rupture of the plantar ligament between the medial cuneiform and the
bases of the second and third metatarsals (Lisfranc ligament) is suggestive of an unstable
midfoot.
Conversely, the appearance of a normal Lisfranc ligament is suggestive of a stable midfoot25
(Resource 5).
CT of the Foot
CT of the foot is the mainstay of advanced imaging for bony involvement and aids in
identifying and quantifying avulsion fractures, articular step-off, subtle instability, and fracture
displacement.

CT of the Foot
Standard CT protocols consist of 2- to 3-mm cuts, with images obtained in axial, coronal,
and sagittal planes. Various imaging windows are used depending on the structures of
interest, with most orthopaedic surgeons favoring the bone window. CT scans are less
helpful with regard to acute ligamentous, tendon, or cartilage injuries, except in patients
with bone involvement, degenerative changes, or associated instability. CT scans also
play a key role in fibrous and bony hindfoot coalitions, which often present as ankle-
related chief complaints and injuries.

9/3/26, 4:26 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001184

With regard to sports medicine injuries, CT scans are diagnostically helpful in patients
with a subtle midfoot injury and patients with an anterior process of the calcaneus
fracture because these injuries often are difficult to appreciate on standard foot
radiographs, especially in the acute setting (Figure 16).
The clinical use of weight-bearing CT has increased for diagnostic and pre-operative
planning purposes. Weight-bearing CT improves on standard CT by revealing the
articular relationships during loading. Weight-bearing CT has grown in application to
better appreciate complex foot and ankle deformity, especially with regard to subtalar
alignment and rotational and angular alignment.18
Figure 16 Sagittal CT scan of a foot shows an anterior process of the calcaneus fracture.
(Courtesy of Brian C. Lau, MD, Durham, NC.)
MRI of the Foot
MRI of the foot provides additional detail on soft tissues of the foot, including ligaments,
tendons, masses, and edema or inflammation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:26 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Lower Extremity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001184
25/30

MRI is particularly useful for patients in whom concern for stress reactions or stress fractures
exists.

MRI of the Foot
MRI of the foot complements the previously mentioned imaging modalities by providing
increasing detail of the soft tissues, including ligament, tendon, masses, and
neurovascular structures, as well as fluid changes that may represent edema and
inflammation. With regard to sports-related injuries of the foot, MRI of the foot is most
useful with regard to stress reactions and fractures.
Standard MRI protocols include axial, coronal, and sagittal planes with 2- to 4-mm cuts26
(Resource 6).T1- and T2-weighted (fluid-sensitive) images typically are obtained in all
three planes. Stress reactions and fractures are commonly observed in the second
metatarsal, fifth metatarsal, navicular, great toe sesamoids, and the calcaneus.27,28 T1-
weighted images will reveal stress fracture lines, which will be dark on T1-weighted
images if present. Conversely, fluid-sensitive sequences (eg, T2-weighted and short tau
inversion recovery images) will demonstrate bone edema and stress reactions, which will
show as increased signal.27 Figure 17 shows an AP radiograph, axial T1-weighted MRI,
and axial T2-weighted MRI of a foot with a stress fracture, revealing associated increased
bone edema in a zone III, fifth metatarsal base fracture.
In addition, anterior process of the calcaneal fractures also may be first identified on MRI
because of their occult nature on plain radiographs. MRI of anterior process of calcaneal
fractures also may suggest the mechanism of injury between avulsion injuries and
impaction injuries across the calcaneocuboid joint.29 Overall, MRIs of the foot should be
carefully scrutinized for bony and associated soft-tissue injuries of the foot. A detailed
understanding of foot anatomy is critical to accurate MRI interpretation of sports-related
injuries.
